title: Spritesheet animation
author: dustyrude
selftext:
What’s currently the best way to create/animate sprites animation for a 2D game?

I already have a GPT subscription, but I haven’t been able to get consistent, usable sprite animations from it. I’ve also looked at several paid AI suites, but most seem pretty expensive considering how few generations you actually get.

I tried running SpriteSheep locally, but the results were hit-or-miss: around 4 minutes per generation, inconsistent quality, and the background removal often wasn’t clean.

Has anyone found a good workflow/tool for generating consistent sprite animations that are actually usable in a game? Local or cloud-based is fine.

comments.author: ZodyXL8
comments.body: Friend, a technique I discovered while desperately searching here, haha, was this: I create the sprite image, animate that sprite in a video AI with it walking or moving Whatever you want, then you take that animated video to the AI you use and ask it to extract a sprite from the video frame by frame.

replies.author: dustyrude
replies.body: that's a nice idea! which ai you used to animate?

replies.author: ZodyXL8
replies.body: I use DOLA AI, but it's annoying because dealing with copyrighted content is really difficult. For instance, I'm creating a Pokémon fangame, and the mere fact that I use the word "Pokémon" in the prompt means it won't generate the animation. Still, it's a great tool to get started with.

replies.author: mxblacksmith
replies.body: This is my exact workflow as well. Image with green screen (chroma key) background, then seedance for image 2 video, then SpriteForge (found on itch.io) to extract and dedupe the frames and pack the sprite atlas.

replies.author: dustyrude
replies.body: do u think buying aseprite and then give the mcp to GPT6 could work also?

replies.author: mxblacksmith
replies.body:
You don't need Aseprite if you are using GPT6 as pixel art is just any other code that AI can do programatically by itself and doesn't need a pixel editor for that. 

I tried GPT6 astra with it, but still the results are not that really good. The best workflow is image to video. Then extract the frames.

replies.author: dustyrude
replies.body: Oh okay, my idea was to use the mcp to animate not to create

replies.author: Lifegem
replies.body: I haven’t been able to generate a true pixel art piece via GPT at all. It pushes out some janky pixel-esque image that will recognize its own error when told, but fails to ever improve even with clear prompting.

comments.author: milox88
comments.body: Ripped a complete motion animation Atlas from AN old game (PNG frame by frame). Gave It to Chatgpt, setting boundaries (like max 8 frame per walk right), let it generate the frame using the ripped One as a mannequin reference. Confronted both source and output in a dedicated built in tool. Animated via opentoonz/krita. Not the best result, but more fluid than a simple prompt "make this character walk, don't mess It up"

comments.author: RsetX
comments.body: Hi! Sprite Sheep creator here. Inconsistency could be due to prompt issues. Try to upload the start sprite in Claude and ask to write the prompt according to Minimax H3 specifications. Background removal can be improved, I suggest to use a chroma key green screen and remove it in game with a shader. Let me know

comments.author: Patient-Sprinkles920
comments.body: I find using Grok Imagine with a reference image works well.

replies.author: dustyrude
replies.body: Grok Image is paid version right?

replies.author: Patient-Sprinkles920
replies.body: yes, and if you give it a reference image or images you reference them by hitting @ and then picking the image, "pose the character from u/image1 as if they are jumping" that way you get complete consistency. You can also turn the image into a video on Grok and then have Claude do screen captures based on your prompt.
